beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Mia has six stickers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Leo has three times as many stickers as Mia. How many does Leo have?

do.text: Mia has 6 stickers. Leo has 3 times as many. How many does Leo have?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Nine! Six plus three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine is a real answer. But it answers a different sentence.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: It answers this one: Leo has three more than Mia.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Mia's strip of six comes down.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Leo adds a small piece of three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Six, and three more. Nine.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: That's just what I did!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. That is a plus story.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now the other sentence: Leo has three times as many.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Times as many does not add a small piece. It copies Mia's whole strip.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: All of Mia's six slides down. That is one time.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Copy the whole strip again, right beside it. Two times. Twelve.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And once more. Three times. Eighteen.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Whoa. Eighteen is way more than nine!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Mia's strip stays on top for scale. Three more makes nine. Three times as many makes eighteen.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So Leo has eighteen stickers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A different question. Mia has six marbles, and Leo has twenty four.

do.text: Mia has 6 marbles. Leo has 24. Leo has how many times as many as Mia?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Leo has eighteen more!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: True. Eighteen more. But the question asks for times as many.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That means: how many copies of Mia's six make Leo's twenty four?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Lay Mia's strip along Leo's. One. Two. Three. Four. It fits exactly four times.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twenty four divided by six is four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check it. Four times six is twenty four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Leo has four times as many marbles as Mia.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So eighteen more, and four times as many. Both are true!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Both true. One compares by taking away. The other compares by copying.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now the smaller amount is missing. Leo has thirty five stickers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is five times as many as Mia has. How many does Mia have?

do.text: Leo has 35 stickers, 5 times as many as Mia. How many does Mia have?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Mia's amount is hiding, so we mark it with a question mark.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Leo has five times as many. So five of Mia's strips, end to end, make Leo's. Two. Three. Four. Five strips in all.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So if I cut Leo's thirty five into five equal pieces, each piece is Mia's!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. Thirty five shared into five equal pieces. Seven in each.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check by copying: five times seven is thirty five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Mia has seven stickers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A multiplication can be read as a comparison. Take three times twenty four is seventy two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is one strip of twenty four. Slide a copy down. And another copy.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three copies of twenty four, and that is seventy two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: So seventy two is three times as many as twenty four, exactly.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: But look down the columns. Every column has three squares!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. One column of three, and another, and another, all the way along to twenty four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twenty four copies of three. So seventy two is also twenty four times as many as three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One multiplication, two comparisons. It works for every one. Thirty five equals five times seven says thirty five is five times as many as seven, and seven times as many as five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now a story, and we choose the equations. Leo has twenty eight stickers, four times as many as Mia.

do.text: Leo has 28 stickers, 4 times as many as Mia. Let $m$ be the number Mia has.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Let *m* be the number Mia has. The letter stands for the amount we do not know.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Leo's twenty eight is four copies of Mia's. One. Two. Three. Four. That is four copies of *m*.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four copies of *m* make twenty eight. So four times *m* equals twenty eight fits.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Or share twenty eight into four equal pieces. Twenty eight divided by four equals *m* fits too.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: What about twenty eight plus four equals *m*?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That says Mia has more than Leo. She has less. It does not fit.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And *m* plus four equals twenty eight?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is a four more story: one small piece of four, not four whole copies. It does not fit.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twenty eight divided by four is seven. Mia has seven stickers.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One last picture: a table of three counts.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four apples, twelve pears, twenty four plums.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We can compare any two. Draw each count as a strip, and let the apple strip be our unit.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Pears first. How many apple strips fit? One. Two. Three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twelve is three times as many as four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now plums. The first twelve are exactly the pears.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: And the next twelve are the pears again. Plums are two times as many as pears.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: And there are six apple strips in the plums!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. Plums are six times as many as apples. One count, three different comparisons.

parts.label: \text{3 times as many: copy the whole}

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here are the two sentences again, with Mia's strip on top for scale.

do.text: More adds a piece. Times as many copies the whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three more. Six plus three is nine. One small piece added.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three times as many. Three times six is eighteen. The whole strip, copied three times.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: So when I hear times as many, I copy the whole thing. I do not just add.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That is it. More adds a piece.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Times as many copies the whole amount.
